extracted.intended_audience: law students, administrative law scholars, judges, lawyers, and interested members of the public
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive account of the Major Questions Doctrine in United States administrative law: its formulations (narrow Chevron-exception vs. broad clear-statement rule), leading cases, indicia of when it applies, and constitutional/interpretive justifications. Includes illustrative case examples showing how courts identify 'major' delegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core rule — requirement of clear and explicit authorization for major questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of major political or economic significance may not be delegated by Congress to executive agencies absent sufficiently clear and explicit authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central formulation: courts look for 'clear congressional authorization' before accepting agency assertions of power in 'extraordinary cases' (quoted language from cases such as Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA and West Virginia v. EPA). Examples: West Virginia v. EPA (2022) requiring agencies to point to clear congressional authorization; Brown & Williamson (2000) urging 'common sense' about delegation on issues of great magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow version — major questions as an exception to Chevron deference
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrow form treats the major questions doctrine as an exception to Chevron deference: on truly major questions, courts will not defer to a reasonable agency interpretation of ambiguous statutory text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Chevron's two-step framework ordinarily, but on 'major questions' the court may refuse to find implicit delegation and thus decline Chevron deference. The page cites Chevron v. NRDC (1984) and notes the Roberts Court's increasing skepticism of Chevron (and Loper Bright overruling Chevron in 2024), and Stephen Breyer's early, narrower endorsement of a flexible major-questions approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad version — clear statement rule formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A broader form treats the major questions doctrine as a clear-statement rule: statutes should not be read to delegate authority to decide major questions unless the statute's text clearly and explicitly grants that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court in cases such as Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA (2014) and West Virginia v. EPA (2022) has expressed an expectation that 'We expect Congress to speak clearly if it wishes to assign to an agency decisions of vast "economic and political significance."' This version functions as a textual canon: look for unmistakable statutory language before recognizing sweeping delegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elephants-in-mouseholes principle (no hiding fundamental changes in vague terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A related canon holding that Congress 'does not alter the fundamental details of a regulatory scheme in vague terms or ancillary provisions' — i.e., it does not 'hide elephants in mouseholes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originates in Whitman v. American Trucking Ass'ns, Inc. (2001) (Scalia). Use this principle to reject readings that infer transformative authority from ancillary or vaguely worded provisions. It functions as an interpretive warning against reading sweeping powers into small or ancillary text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of a 'major question' or transformative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors courts consider in labeling an issue a 'major question' include whether the agency's interpretation would (a) assert transformative or unprecedented regulatory authority, (b) have vast economic or political significance, (c) sweep in large sectors or 'millions' of entities, or (d) alter the balance between federal and state power or affect private-property rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: UARG rejected extending 'air pollutants' to CO2 because it would regulate 'millions[] of small sources nationwide'; West Virginia characterized EPA's generation-shifting approach as a 'transformative expansion' and 'unheralded power'; Alabama Ass'n of Realtors noted intrusion into landlord-tenant law and alteration of federal-state balance. These indicia are used as practical signals that courts should demand clearer congressional authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that courts demand more than a 'merely plausible textual basis' in extraordinary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In 'extraordinary cases' courts require something more than a merely plausible textual basis for agency action — agencies must point to clear congressional authorization for the power they claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted language from Utility Air (and cited in West Virginia) establishes that in such cases the agency cannot rely on a marginal or arguable textual basis; the bar for showing delegation is materially higher. This guidance is applied to avoid upholding agency actions based on slender textual readings when the consequences are large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional/separation-of-powers justification (overlap with nondelegation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine is sometimes justified as serving separation-of-powers concerns: it prevents Congress from divesting itself of legislative power by delegating truly legislative choices to agencies without clear authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Justices (e.g., Gorsuch, Roberts in certain writings) and commentators treat the major questions doctrine as feeding into nondelegation principles or as a proxy for constitutional limits. The page notes disagreements about whether it is merely a canon of statutory construction or a constitutional rule and cites Gorsuch's and others' statements linking the doctrine to constitutional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive tools/examples — 'common sense' and contextual reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts sometimes invoke 'common sense' and contextual considerations (rather than strict textualism) to decide whether Congress intended to delegate authority over major issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brown & Williamson (2000) advised using 'common sense' about how Congress is likely to delegate issues of economic and political magnitude. Justice Barrett (in Biden v. Nebraska concurrence) described the doctrine as a contextual and intuitive linguistic canon for determining plain meaning. Use of 'common sense' means courts may weigh legislative context, history, and implications when assessing delegation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical consequences as a test (irreversibility and reliance costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may consider real-world consequences — such as reliance interests and the irreversibility or costliness of compliance — when deciding whether an agency's claimed power is likely one Congress intended to delegate implicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites concerns expressed in court memos about not allowing rules to take effect and impose compliance costs before final judicial decision (e.g., the Roberts memo worried about Michigan v. EPA allowing rules to go into effect and making them effectively irreversible). Such practical considerations can push courts to require clearer statutory authorization for sweeping regulatory actions.
